questions.question: Q: How has streaming changed television as a media form?

points.text: Streaming has changed TV by: removing scheduling (audiences watch on demand), enabling binge-watching of entire series, using data to commission targeted content, increasing production budgets for 'quality TV', and creating global distribution. However, traditional broadcast TV still reaches mass audiences for live events.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between public service and commercial television?

points.text: Public service TV (BBC, Channel 4) is funded by the licence fee or public ownership and has a remit to inform, educate, and entertain diverse audiences. Commercial TV (ITV, Sky) is funded by advertising and subscription, prioritising content that attracts large audiences and revenue. This affects the types of programmes each produces.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Contemporary TV drama uses a range of conventions to engage audiences, combining traditional narrative techniques with innovations driven by streaming. Enigma codes are central to audience engagement — unanswered questions drive viewers to keep watching. In many TV dramas, each episode ends with a cliffhanger that creates narrative suspense, while longer series arcs develop mysteries across multiple episodes. Barthes argued that enigma codes are the 'engine' of narrative, and TV drama relies heavily on them. Multi-strand narratives engage audiences by interweaving different storylines, creating complexity that rewards sustained viewing. Streaming services have amplified this convention — series designed for binge-watching can develop more complex narratives across an entire season, since audiences watch episodes in quick succession rather than waiting a week. Character-driven narratives are a key convention of 'quality TV'. Complex, morally ambiguous protagonists engage audiences emotionally and intellectually — viewers debate characters' motivations and decisions on social media, extending engagement beyond the screen. Visual conventions including cinematic camerawork, production design, and colour grading create a sense of quality that distinguishes 'peak TV' from standard broadcasting.
